headline.main: Using AI to Humiliate Women: The Men Behind Deepfake Pornography
headline.social: Using AI to Humiliate Women: The Men Behind Deepfake Pornography

intro: AI-generated naked images of real women is the business model behind Clothoff, a dubious "nudify" app that has millions of visitors. Now, a whistleblower has provided details of just how cynical the site's operators are.
text:
Miriam Al Adib is still furious. "The operators of Clothoff only care about money. They are clearly uninterested about the consequences of their app for young women.” The Spanish gynecologist knows what she’s talking about. In September 2023, faked naked pictures of her daughter, who was 14 years old at the time, were produced using the artificial intelligence tool offered by the app Clothoff. The images were circulated in local WhatsApp groups in the family’s hometown and the 14-year-old was approached on the street about the pictures and bullied by boys. "If I didn’t know what my daughter looked like naked, I would have thought the pictures were real,” says Al Adib.
Her daughter wasn’t the only victim. At least 20 girls between the ages of 11 and 17 from four different schools in the Spanish town of Almendralejo were stripped naked against their will with the help of the app. Their parents joined forces to fight back.
Naked pictures generated with the help of AI are a new and often overlooked form of cyber-mobbing, says Al Adib. "Such AI images can be extremely dangerous to the psyches of young people,” says the doctor, who leads several women’s health practices in Spain. "The thought immediately occurred to me: There have already been cases where victims of cyber-bullying have killed themselves out of desperation," Al Adib says, recalling her shock upon seeing the fake naked pictures of her daughter. DER SPIEGEL first reported on the globally growing problem of deepfake porn  in December 2024. Now, statements and documents from an insider reveal how lucrative the business is – and how shameless the people behind it are.
Young women in Germany have also become victims of such attacks. "I know of schools where boys have created fake naked images of their classmates to torment them and to damage their reputations,” says media pedagogue Saskia Nakari of the state media center in Baden-Württemberg. She educates teachers and parents about the risks of crossing digital boundaries and produces a podcast on the topic. In addition to the traumatic consequences for the victims, such apps also convey a dangerously inaccurate image of sexuality, says Nakari. Still, she says, some schools don’t take the problem seriously enough. "I’m afraid that there could soon be more cases of bullying using fake nude images because of advances in AI.”
The perpetrators in Spain come from a group of 15 underage local boys. In the case of Al Adib’s daughter, they took a real photo from her freely accessible WhatsApp status and uploaded it to Clothoff. The app’s AI program produced a nude image. For other girls, they took photos from their Instagram accounts or photographed themselves as they were playing volleyball.
The boys have since been given suspended sentences of one year for the dissemination of child pornography. Because the verdicts were handed down by a juvenile court, details have not been made public about which of the boys was responsible for what share of the crime. Al Adib is ultimately satisfied with how the case was handled in the town, with the parents of the two sides reaching an agreement in court, she says. "The girls received justice and hopefully the boys have learned something.”
What Al Adib refuses to accept is that the case has thus far had no consequences whatsoever for the people behind Clothoff. "I find it unethical that crimes like the one against my daughter and many other girls around the world can continue to be committed,” she told DER SPIEGEL in an interview in early June.
Clothoff is a so-called nudify app. A flourishing global market for such services has developed, with far more than 60 such offerings launching in the last two years. All of them work in basically the same way: The AI used by the app makes it possible with just a few clicks to transform a normal snapshot into a bikini picture or a completely naked image. Such deepfakes of unsuspecting women have become one of the underreported downsides of the generative AI boom in recent years.
Nudify apps are not hidden in obscure forums or on pornography platforms, rather they are freely available on the internet. The only limitation: Many of these services only work with women’s bodies. The AI programs they use have apparently never been trained to produce naked pictures of men. Images of women in underwear are usually free, with faked photos of subjects in typical pornographic poses available for a price of just a few euros.
Clothoff is one of the leading apps on the market. In just the first six months of 2024, the website received 27 million visitors, with an average of 200,000 pictures being produced by the program each day, according to the company. Thousands of women have likely become victims of the app. The creators of Clothoff are among the most unscrupulous nudify operators and offer photo montages with schoolgirl outfits and pregnant women in sex poses. The app has recently begun marketing the ability to create fake videos with a picture. According to company information, the function has already been used over a million times.
In August 2024, public officials in San Francisco, California went public with a lawsuit against Clothoff and several other nudify apps. They demanded that the services cease operation due to the distribution of child and youth pornography. The investigators from the heart of Silicon Valley were likely also motivated by the fact that cases had become public at several schools in the state in which AI-generated nude images of girls had been circulated. Thus far, however, officials have experienced only moderate success in identifying the people behind the apps or getting them to suspend their services. The operators of Clothoff, in any case, seem unimpressed by the lawsuit.
The Whistleblower
Just how lucrative Clothoff’s business has become can now be seen by the statements of a whistleblower who has access to internal company information. Working for the app, he says, initially felt like being part of an exciting startup. "But over time, people became just cynical and obsessed with money.” For his own safety and out of concern that the company may seek to retaliate, his identity cannot be revealed. He, too, initially joined the project in the hopes that it would turn out to be profitable, but he now feels partly responsible for what Clothoff has become. Which is why he is going public with his information.
"Clothoff has bought up an entire network of nudify apps,” the whistleblower says. DER SPIEGEL reporting, using online evidence and extracts from the commercial register, has confirmed that Clothoff now owns 10 other nudify services, all of them with monthly views ranging between hundreds of thousands to several million.
The annual budget of Clothoff alone, the whistleblower says, is 3 million euros. Files that he made available to DER SPIEGEL show that more than three dozen people work for the company. Just how professionally and brazenly the company acts can be seen by plans for a new, large-scale marketing plan aimed at the German market and referred to internally as the "referendum.” There is a clear "timeline for implementation,” outlining precisely when programmers or the social media team must accomplish which steps.
As part of the campaign, Clothoff plans to produce naked images of well-known influencers, singers and actresses. "You choose who you want to undress,” reads the tagline above a list of German stars, according to the planning documents. The winner is to be crowned the "hottest hottie.” The campaign marks something of a strategy shift for Clothoff. Thus far, other platforms have tended to lead the way in the creation of celebrity fakes.
Target Group: Andrew Tate Fans
DER SPIEGEL knows the names of the stars who are apparently being taken advantage of by Clothoff against their will. Several of them have confirmed that they never provided their approval for the campaign or for the use of their images by the AI program. For that reason, we will not be naming them here. People close to several of those affected say they are particularly shocked that an app like Clothoff, which can be used for cyber-bullying at schools, is now apparently planning to use pictures of celebrities for advertising purposes. Several representatives of the stars say they would take legal action if the marketing campaign is indeed launched. None of them wanted to comment further.
Clothoff isn’t just planning such a celebrity-based campaign in Germany, but also for the French, British and Spanish markets. The whistleblower says that the marketing budget is 150,000 euros per country. The money is to be spent on advertising posts in special Telegram channels, in sex subs on Reddit and on 4chan, the channel that has become notorious for its lax regulations. According to the campaign documents, the target group is "men between 16 and 35.” Interests: "video games,” "internet memes,” "right-wing extremist ideas,” "misogyny” and "Andrew Tate” – the influencer who has been promoting misogynistic content to an audience of millions for years.
The people behind Clothoff do their best to conceal their identities. The imprint on the website has displayed alternating addresses: Currently, it is allegedly headquartered on the British Virgin Islands, though it used to claim an address in the Argentinian capital of Buenos Aires. But in summer 2024, the operators made a mistake. They left an internal database publicly available on the internet, through which DER SPIEGEL was able to identify four central people behind the website in countries in Eastern Europe: Alexander G. from Russia, Dascha and Alexander B. from Belarus, and Yevgeniy B. from Ukraine, whose company was mentioned for a time in the Clothoff imprint. The 30-year-old describes himself on the internet as someone who values honesty and family, noting that he works as a web designer and an artist.
The whistleblower confirmed to DER SPIEGEL that all Clothoff employees work in countries that used to belong to the Soviet Union. That is consistent with the fact that all of the company’s internal communications that DER SPIEGEL has in its possession are completely in Russian, and the company’s email service is also based in Russia.
"More of a Garage Startup”
The four central players declined to respond to attempts by DER SPIEGEL to contact them for the story published in December 2024. A person named Elias did get in touch, however, claiming to be a spokesperson for the app. He said the four people mentioned above were unknown to him. Because of a nondisclosure agreement, he said, he was unable to answer questions about the team and about who was responsible for what task at Clothoff. The spokesman also wrote that Clothoff forbids the use of photos of people without their consent and claimed that the service had no connection to the "terrible story” in Almendralejo. Furthermore, he insisted that the website’s technology does not process photos of minors. When asked about the database accidentally left open on the internet, Elias first said that the company did not use the web service associated with the database – but Clothoff took the data off the web after being approached for comment. The name of the database was in Russian and can be translated as "my babe.”
Elias denied that the app has an annual budget of over $3 million. Fewer than 30 people are part of the central team behind the program, he says, adding that they are fighting to even generate a profit. "Think garage startup vibes, not Silicon Valley unicorn,” Elias said.
The people behind the company don’t just strive for anonymity for themselves, they also guarantee it to their users. "We do not save any data,” reads the imprint. That, though, is clearly wrong. An additional source provided DER SPIEGEL with a list of email addresses from thousands of users who have paid money to the app, thus allowing them to make especially explicit images. The list contains numerous customers from German-speaking countries.
One of them is a 49-year-old father from Switzerland. When DER SPIEGEL reached him and asked about Clothoff, a nervous laugh could be heard on the other end of the line. He agreed to talk about his use of the app only on condition that his name not be used. He said he has spent around 40 euros on the app and created naked images and faked sex photos of well-known singers from the U.S. "I wanted to try it out, and of course lust was part of it,” he said, sounding embarrassed.
Some of the images were clearly recognizable as AI fakes, he said, but others looked quite realistic. On one occasion, the app refused to generate a picture because the singer in the photo he was trying to upload looked like she might be underage, the man recalled. Three days later, though, he said, he uploaded the same image and it worked just fine.
When it was pointed out to him that the American singer had never given him permission to create fake sex images of her, he responded: "But there are enough pictures of her on the internet as it is.” The Swiss father didn’t think he had done anything wrong. He said he never shared the images and only saved them locally. He only from DER SPIEGEL, he claimed, that it is illegal to produce such images without consent from the person depicted. "I’m not going to deinstall the app because of it.” He claimed, though, that he would never take pictures of private individuals and upload them to Clothoff. "If I ever learned of someone producing such photos of my daughter, I would be horrified.”
With reporting by Christo Buschek and Roman Höfner
